Is the photography service still worth funding?¶

From historical data to an experiment that includes the restaurant's decisions and the competition¶

Part 1 of the Data Science challenge · Just Eat · Working proposal

A restaurant publishes new photos, raises prices and receives more orders. That may be good news for the restaurant. We still do not know how much the platform gained, what happened to its competitors, or whether customers got a better experience. And the photographer's cost has yet to be subtracted.

This story has two parts. First we explore the past as a supporting study: we learn which comparisons could be defensible and how much the precision depends on the assumptions. Then we design the main prospective experiment: randomising immediate or deferred access to the service across cities or metropolitan areas, keeping requests voluntary and prices free.

The retrospective study can inform the choice of metrics, the variability and the timelines. It does not replace random assignment, nor does it force us to discard an experiment if its historical comparisons are not credible.

Section Question it answers
Part I · §§ 1–12 What could we learn from historical data, under what assumptions and with what precision?
Bridge · § 13 Why does an A/B test of images at current prices answer only part of the question?
Part II · §§ 14–26 How do we assign, measure, size and analyse the future experiment?
Closing · § 27 What remains open and what would improve the proposal?

Shortcuts: sample size calculation · power simulation.

Reading contract. We have no internal Just Eat records. The public figures provide scale and carry a date; they are not an experimental sample. The examples, charts and simulations are synthetic. Every operational or statistical assumption is identified as a proposal or a scenario: no sample size, timeline or causal result is presented as validated against real data.

Part I · The past as a supporting study¶

1. The question starts with an outcome we never observe¶

Suppose a restaurant goes from 100 to 140 weekly orders after publishing photographs. We know it gained 40 orders. To attribute them to the photos we need to answer something we do not observe: how many orders would that same restaurant have received, on those same dates, without publishing them? That alternative history is called the counterfactual.

We look for similar restaurants that have not published yet. In the example, they go from 100 to 120 orders. They help us approximate what might have happened without the photos:

Step Calculation Interpretation
Change among those who publish 140 − 100 = 40 Includes the photos and any other change in context
Change among those still waiting 120 − 100 = 20 Approximates the growth there would have been without photos
Difference between those changes 40 − 20 = 20 Effect attributable to the photos if the comparison is valid

Hence the name difference-in-differences: we compute two changes and then subtract them. We will call those who publish the treated group and those serving as a comparison without publishing during those dates the controls.

The key condition is parallel trends: without new photos, both groups would have changed in a similar way, on the chosen metric. They can start from different sales levels. What has to be comparable is how they evolve without the intervention, within the context we are analysing.

For example, if only the restaurants that publish also take part in a local campaign, the waiting group no longer represents their evolution without photos well. Looking at earlier weeks and knowing the campaigns helps assess the comparison, but similar prior trends do not prove the assumption.

Show reproducible code
weeks = np.arange(-8, 9)
common = 100 + 2.5 * weeks
treated = common + np.where(weeks > 0, 2.5 * weeks, 0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.8))
ax.axvspan(0, 8.7, color=ORANGE, alpha=.055)
ax.plot(weeks, common, color=TEAL, linewidth=3, label="Comparison: still without photos")
ax.plot(weeks, treated, color=ORANGE, linewidth=3, label="Publish photographs")
ax.axvline(0, color=MUTED, linestyle=":", linewidth=1.5)
ax.annotate("Publication", (0, 83), xytext=(.4, 83), fontsize=10)
ax.annotate("", xy=(8.25, 140), xytext=(8.25, 120),
            arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "<->", "color": INK, "lw": 1.5})
ax.text(8.55, 130, "+20 pedidos\natribuibles*", va="center", fontsize=10)
ax.set(xlim=(-8, 11.3), ylim=(75, 148), xlabel="Weeks relative to publication",
       ylabel="Pedidos semanales medios")
ax.set_title("El aumento observado mezcla el efecto de las fotos y el del contexto", pad=14)
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=10)
ax.grid(axis="y", color=GRID)
finish(fig, "01_contrafactual", "Synthetic example · *Causal interpretation only if the design assumptions hold")

2. The waiting list offers a candidate comparison¶

Restaurants that request the service already share a decision: they want to improve their photos. We can compare those who publish earlier with those still waiting, provided we understand why some were served first.

If the sales rep prioritised whoever was about to launch a big promotion, sales may rise because of that promotion. If the delay is due to logistical availability unrelated to sales prospects, the comparison may be more defensible. That independence has to be investigated; it does not follow from the mere existence of delays.

A calendar example. Two similar restaurants request the service on 2 January. A publishes on 16 January and B on 27 February. Between 16 January and 12 February we can observe four weeks with photos at A and without photos at B. We compare their changes against a shared earlier period, measured before any effects of the request itself. Comparing A in January with B in August would introduce a different season and context.

Finding that pair is called matching. We use prior characteristics — also called covariates — such as cuisine type, area, price, tenure, existing photos and order trajectory. Here, a market is an area or set of restaurants sharing customers and demand conditions; a country can contain many distinct markets.

Matching helps choose who to compare with; DiD compares how they evolve. If we have not recorded that an owner was preparing a campaign, that factor can keep biasing the comparison even with good matching.

Because each restaurant publishes on a different date, we speak of staggered adoption. A cohort groups those who publish in a similar period. We will accumulate comparisons within the same year, keeping the same calendar weeks in each comparison. B stops serving as a control when it publishes, or earlier if it already starts changing its behaviour because of the intervention: that is called anticipation. Windows can cross the year boundary if there are data and valid controls.

Show reproducible code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5.3))
cohorts = [("Enero", 1), ("Abril", 14), ("Julio", 27), ("Octubre", 40)]
for k, (label, request) in enumerate(cohorts):
    y = 7 - 2*k
    early, late, horizon = request + 2, request + 8, 4
    ax.plot([request, early], [y, y], color=GRID, lw=7, solid_capstyle="round")
    ax.plot([request, late], [y-0.65, y-0.65], color=GRID, lw=7, solid_capstyle="round")
    ax.plot([early, early+horizon], [y, y], color=ORANGE, lw=8, solid_capstyle="butt")
    ax.plot([early, early+horizon], [y-.65, y-.65], color=TEAL, lw=8, solid_capstyle="butt")
    ax.scatter([early, late], [y, y-.65], color=INK, s=35, zorder=4)
    ax.text(request-.6, y+.35, label, fontsize=10, weight="bold")
    ax.text(early+horizon+.6, y, "Con fotos", fontsize=9, va="center", color=ORANGE)
    ax.text(late+.6, y-.65, "Publishes later", fontsize=9, va="center", color=MUTED)
ax.set(xlim=(-1, 58), ylim=(-.2, 8.2), yticks=[], xlabel="Weeks within the same year")
ax.set_title("Valid comparisons accumulate, without requiring a single publication date", pad=14)
ax.plot([], [], color=ORANGE, lw=6, label="Ventana observada: publica antes")
ax.plot([], [], color=TEAL, lw=6, label="Mismas semanas: sigue esperando")
ax.legend(loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0, -.02), fontsize=9, ncol=2)
finish(fig, "02_cohortes", "Calendario ilustrativo · Cada par contiene restaurantes distintos · Ventana posterior de 4 semanas")

What question this comparison answers, exactly¶

We would estimate the effect of publishing earlier, during the weeks when other comparable applicants have still not published. For instance: the effect over the first four weeks among restaurants similar to A and B. That period is the follow-up horizon, and those restaurants form the study population.

The result does not automatically extend to those who never requested the service, nor does it directly describe what would happen if Just Eat shut it down: existing photos would remain and restaurants could adapt.

To estimate it we would use a DiD by cohort and date with not-yet-treated controls, along the lines of Callaway and Sant'Anna. One important technical precaution is not to automatically turn a restaurant that has had photos for months into a control for another that has just published them: the first may still be receiving an effect from the photos. With effects that vary across restaurants or over time, those comparisons can distort the result (Goodman-Bacon).

We also distinguish prior characteristics from consequences of the photos. If the images increase clicks and that improves the restaurant's ranking in the app, adjusting for that downstream ranking can remove part of the total effect we wanted to measure. That is why we fix the adjustment variables before the intervention.

3. Sushi and pizza: adding up without adjusting can invent an effect¶

Now imagine two cuisine types with different trends. Without new photos, pizza grows 10 % and sushi 30 %. The photos add 5 percentage points in both cases: going from 10 % to 15 % is 5 points, which we will abbreviate 5 pp. These are differences between percentages, not a 5 % relative increase.

Cuisine type Growth without new photos Growth with photos Effect within the cuisine type
Pizza 10 % 15 % +5 pp
Sushi 30 % 35 % +5 pp

But 80 % of those who publish are sushi restaurants, against only 20 % of those still waiting. The aggregate calculation gives:

  • Publishers: 20 % × 15 % + 80 % × 35 % = 31 % average growth.
  • Waiting: 80 % × 10 % + 20 % × 30 % = 14 % average growth.
  • Unadjusted comparison: 31 % − 14 % = 17 pp, even though the photos contribute 5 pp in each cuisine type.

We are mixing the effect of the photos with the fact that one group contains more restaurants from the segment that was already growing faster. All these figures are invented to explain the problem; they do not describe real sushi or pizza businesses.

Show reproducible code
control_change = np.array([.10, .30])
treated_change = control_change + .05
mix_t, mix_c = np.array([.20, .80]), np.array([.80, .20])
naive = (mix_t @ treated_change) - (mix_c @ control_change)
adjusted = np.mean(treated_change - control_change)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.7), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.4, 1]})
x, width = np.arange(2), .30
axes[0].bar(x-width/2, control_change*100, width, color=TEAL, label="Esperan")
axes[0].bar(x+width/2, treated_change*100, width, color=ORANGE, label="Publican")
axes[0].set(xticks=x, xticklabels=["Pizza", "Sushi"], ylim=(0, 42), ylabel="Crecimiento de pedidos (%)")
axes[0].set_title("Dentro de cada tipo de comida\n+5 puntos", pad=12)
axes[0].legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=10)
axes[0].grid(axis="y", color=GRID)
axes[0].set_axisbelow(True)
axes[1].bar([0, 1], [naive*100, adjusted*100], color=[RED, TEAL], width=.55)
axes[1].set(xticks=[0, 1], xticklabels=["Mezcla\nsin ajustar", "Comparison\nby cuisine type"],
            ylim=(0, 21), ylabel="Diferencia estimada (puntos porcentuales)")
axes[1].set_title("The mix changes the conclusion", pad=12)
for i, v in enumerate([naive*100, adjusted*100]):
    axes[1].text(i, v+.5, f"{v:.0f} pp", ha="center", weight="bold")
finish(fig, "03_composicion")

The solution is to compare sushi with sushi and pizza with pizza first. Then we can combine the effects. The importance we give each segment is its weight: if we want to represent a population that is 80 % pizzerias, a per-restaurant average will give 80 % of the weight to that segment. In this example any common mix gives 5 pp, because the effect is identical in both cuisine types; with real data it could differ.

Splitting the sample into comparable groups is called stratifying, and each group is a stratum. It does not make restaurants disappear by itself. The difficulty arises when a restaurant finds no comparable counterpart in the waiting group.

That is common support: having restaurants from both groups with similar prior characteristics. If every sushi restaurant in a given market already has photos and the only ones waiting are pizzerias at a different price level, we have no adequate comparison there. Predicting what would have happened to the sushi restaurants from the pizzerias would be extrapolation: extending the result to a situation with no observed comparison.

The usable sample can shrink through lack of support or through matches that are too distant. A different requirement is asking for a precise result for each segment: there each answer rests on less information. Later on we will compute both cases without conflating them.

4. A large platform does not imply a large causal sample¶

The 2024 annual report states 95,000 partner outlets in Northern Europe and 100,000 in the United Kingdom and Ireland; these include restaurants and other retailers. Just Eat Italy reported more than 28,000 restaurants in June 2024. The indicative total exceeds 223,000 outlets without counting Spain and other markets, with differing dates and definitions.

Sources: 2024 annual report, reproduction of the corporate document and Just Eat Italy press release.

We will use 200,000 restaurants as a hypothetical universe for the calculations. It is not an official census of Europe nor a 2023 figure. Nor do we know how many request photos, how long they wait, or whether the programme operates comparably across brands and countries. The public data only justify the order of magnitude.

From the universe to the pairs we can actually compare¶

In our scenario, 3 % request the service: 200,000 × 3 % = 6,000. Of those applicants, we assume 85 % have prior history and reliable dates: 6,000 × 85 % = 5,100. We keep applying filters to whoever remains. Each percentage is conditional on the previous step, which is why they multiply.

We count unique restaurants: a final pair contains one that publishes and one that waits. The balanced-groups assumption means we will have the same number on each side of the comparison.

The parameters can be changed and recomputed. Besides the rates, there are two noise assumptions: the residual standard deviation measures how much sales changes still vary after adjustment; the variance inflation factor represents additional dependence, for example between restaurants in the same market. Section 6 explains how both affect precision.

Show reproducible code
# Working scenario: none of these parameters comes from service records.
P = dict(
    universo=200_000,
    tasa_solicitud=.03,       # Request during one year.
    historial=.85,           # Sufficient PRIOR history and reliable process dates.
    contraste=.40,           # Can support a contemporaneous 4-week comparison.
    soporte=.60,             # Have counterparts on relevant prior covariates.
    emparejamiento=.85,      # Additional retention when building disjoint 1:1 pairs.
    sigma=.30,               # Residual SD of the change in orders: 30 percentage points.
    alpha=.05,               # Two-sided significance.
    potencia=.80,
    inflacion_varianza=1.50, # Sensitivity to dependence; not a measured factor.
    efecto_objetivo=.05,     # 5 percentage points of additional growth.
)

def sample_size(p):
    raw = p["universo"] * np.prod([p[k] for k in
        ["tasa_solicitud", "historial", "contraste", "soporte", "emparejamiento"]])
    return 2 * int(np.floor(raw / 2))  # Disjoint pairs: one restaurant in each group.

def standard_error(total, sigma=.30, inflation=1):
    # Two groups of size total/2: Var(difference) = 4*sigma^2/total.
    return 2 * sigma * np.sqrt(inflation / np.asarray(total))

def detectable_effect(total, sigma=.30, alpha=.05, power=.80, inflation=1):
    return (norm.ppf(1-alpha/2) + norm.ppf(power)) * standard_error(total, sigma, inflation)

def required_total(effect, sigma=.30, alpha=.05, power=.80, inflation=1):
    z = norm.ppf(1-alpha/2) + norm.ppf(power)
    return 2 * int(np.ceil(2*z*z*sigma*sigma*inflation / effect**2))

def achieved_power(total, effect, sigma=.30, alpha=.05, inflation=1):
    z = norm.ppf(1-alpha/2)
    noncentrality = effect / standard_error(total, sigma, inflation)
    return norm.sf(z-noncentrality) + norm.cdf(-z-noncentrality)

N = sample_size(P)
MDE = detectable_effect(N, P["sigma"], P["alpha"], P["potencia"], P["inflacion_varianza"])
POWER = achieved_power(N, P["efecto_objetivo"], P["sigma"], P["alpha"], P["inflacion_varianza"])

rows = [
    ("Hypothetical universe", integer(P["universo"])),
    ("Requests / year", f'{P["tasa_solicitud"]:.0%}'),
    ("Historial y fechas fiables", f'{P["historial"]:.0%}'),
    ("Contemporaneous 4-week comparison", f'{P["contraste"]:.0%}'),
    ("Common support", f'{P["soporte"]:.0%}'),
    ("Additional retention on matching", f'{P["emparejamiento"]:.0%}'),
    ("DE residual del cambio", f'{P["sigma"]*100:.0f} pp'),
    ("Variance inflation factor", f'{P["inflacion_varianza"]:.2f}'),
]
show_table(pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["Parameter", "Supuesto editable"]))
Parameter Supuesto editable
Hypothetical universe 200.000
Requests / year 3%
Historial y fechas fiables 85%
Contemporaneous 4-week comparison 40%
Common support 60%
Additional retention on matching 85%
DE residual del cambio 30 pp
Variance inflation factor 1.50
Show reproducible code

          "Contrapartes comparables", "Pares finales disjuntos"]
rates = [P["tasa_solicitud"], P["historial"], P["contraste"], P["soporte"], P["emparejamiento"]]
counts = P["universo"] * np.cumprod(rates)
counts[-1] = N
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5.1))
bars = ax.barh(labels, counts, color=["#CFD8DA", "#AFBEC2", "#899FA6", "#4C7F89", ORANGE], height=.60)
ax.invert_yaxis()
for b, v in zip(bars, counts):
    ax.text(v+max(counts)*.018, b.get_y()+b.get_height()/2, integer(v), va="center", weight="bold")
ax.set_xlim(0, max(counts)*1.19)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(lambda x, _: integer(x)))

display(Markdown(
    f'El escenario conserva **{integer(N)} restaurantes: {integer(N//2)} por grupo**. '
    f'Equivalen al **{N/(P["universo"]*P["tasa_solicitud"]):.1%} de los solicitantes**. '
    'Este porcentaje conjunto es el producto de los filtros supuestos. '
    'We need the service records to replace it with a measurement.'
))

El escenario conserva 1.040 restaurantes: 520 por grupo. Equivalen al 17.3% de los solicitantes. Este porcentaje conjunto es el producto de los filtros supuestos. We need the service records to replace it with a measurement.

The filters describe the availability of comparisons; they are fixed before looking at the effects. We would not exclude a restaurant because its sales fell or it closed: that could be part of the outcome we want to measure. A known closure and a missing record are different situations. The rules for follow-up and for handling missing data must be defined explicitly.

Nor would we count a control ten times for reusing it in ten comparisons. And two restaurants from the same chain can react together to a promotion: their data are correlated, so they contribute less independent information than two unrelated observations. The uncertainty calculation must reflect that.

There is another, distinct problem: if one restaurant gains orders by taking them from another, their outcomes influence each other causally. That is called interference. Correcting the uncertainty calculation for correlation does not remove that contamination of the comparison group.

5. Splitting helps compare; it does not force forty separate studies¶

Each pair we have kept contains one restaurant that publishes and a comparable one that waits. In the map below we distribute those pairs synthetically across eight markets and five cuisine types. A cell with 47 pairs represents 94 restaurants, split between the two groups. A dash indicates that in this example there are no pairs available in that cell; it does not prove the segment does not exist.

We can use the populated cells to compute a single average effect over the represented population. We can also ask for one effect per cell, but then each answer has far less sample behind it. Those two questions require different levels of precision.

With real data we would investigate each gap: perhaps nobody requested the service, perhaps everyone already published, or perhaps we found no sufficiently similar controls. The answer determines which restaurants we can extend the conclusions to.

A note on the real categories. In an exploratory query to the Just Eat API for postcode EC4M7RF, London, made on 14 October 2026, we found 130 distinct tags across 2,054 unique outlets. They mix cuisine types, products, attributes such as "vegan" or "halal", and retailers such as supermarkets or pharmacies. An outlet can carry several tags. Before any analysis they would need to be cleaned and grouped into coherent categories, with a defined treatment for multi-tag cases and an exclusion of retailers outside the study population. These 130 tags correspond to that current query, not to a complete catalogue for Europe nor to the restaurants available in 2023. The five cuisine types in the example remain an illustrative simplification.

Show reproducible code
rng = np.random.default_rng(2023)
market_w = np.array([.26, .19, .15, .12, .10, .08, .06, .04])
cuisine_w = np.array([.31, .23, .18, .16, .12])
weights = np.outer(market_w, cuisine_w)
for i, j in [(0, 4), (2, 1), (4, 3), (5, 4), (6, 2), (7, 0)]:
    weights[i, j] = 0
weights /= weights.sum()
pairs = rng.multinomial(N//2, weights.ravel()).reshape(8, 5)
cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("pairs", ["#F0F1EB", "#A9D4D0", TEAL])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 5.8))
im = ax.imshow(pairs, cmap=cmap, aspect="auto", vmin=0)
for (i, j), v in np.ndenumerate(pairs):
    ax.text(j, i, str(v) if v else "—", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=11,
            color="white" if v > .65*pairs.max() else INK)
ax.set_xticks(np.arange(5), ["Pizza", "Sushi", "Hamburguesas", "Local", "Otros"])
ax.set_yticks(np.arange(8), [f"Mercado {i}" for i in range(1, 9)])
ax.set_title(f'{integer(N//2)} pares pueden aportar a un efecto agregado; cada segmento aporta menos', pad=16)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="Valid pairs in the example", fraction=.035, pad=.04)
finish(fig, "05_segmentos", "Synthetic distribution of already-valid pairs · No further funnel losses applied")

6. How much precision does that sample buy?¶

A valid comparison can still be too noisy. With few restaurants, a normal fluctuation in their sales can look like an improvement caused by the photos, or hide a real one.

First we decide what we want to detect¶

Suppose two restaurants both started at 100 orders per week. The one waiting reaches 110 and the one that publishes reaches 115. They grow 10 % and 15 %: the difference is 5 percentage points, or 5 pp. The five extra orders are 5 % of the initial 100 orders, but 4.5 % of the 110 orders in the counterfactual. That is why we specify the metric and avoid an ambiguous "5 %".

On the back of the napkin we compute, per restaurant, the change in average orders after against before, divided by the before. Then we compare the average growth of both groups. If the initial average is zero or very small, this metric needs a prior rule or an alternative: you cannot divide by zero, nor allow tiny denominators to dominate the analysis.

Concept What it means, with an example Working assumption
Minimum relevant effect, δ The improvement worth distinguishing in order to make the decision. It is a business criterion. 5 pp
Significance, α If there were no effect and we repeated valid studies, we want only about 5 in 100 to declare an effect by chance. That is a false positive. 5 %, two-sided
Power, 1 − β If there really were a 5 pp improvement, we want to detect it in about 80 out of 100 repetitions of the study. 80 %
Minimum detectable effect, MDE The effect size for which our sample reaches that power. It is a capability of the data, not a business preference. We compute it

Two-sided means we allow for both an improvement and a deterioration. α is not the probability that a particular conclusion is false. And an effect smaller than the MDE can still come out significant; we simply have less chance of detecting it than we required.

Power and significance are related. We choose criteria to design the study: limit false alarms and frequently detect a relevant improvement. Then we compute how much sample we need to meet them; writing "80 %" does not guarantee that power. With the same sample, noise and real effect, cutting α from 5 % to 1 % tightens the criterion and reduces power. To recover it, we normally need more information. The p-value is produced by the analysis; we choose the threshold we will compare it against in advance. Neither 5 % nor 80 % is a binding law.

The crucial comparison will be relevant effect against detectable effect: if we need to detect 5 pp and the sample only reaches 80 % power for 6.4 pp, it does not meet the precision objective.

Now we translate the noise into a reproducible calculation¶

To understand residual, imagine the model expects 10 % growth given the market, the season and prior characteristics. If three restaurants grow 18 %, 4 % and 11 %, their residuals are +8, −6 and +1 points. The standard deviation of those residuals summarises their spread. The example only explains the term; it is not how the 30-point assumption was derived.

σ = 0.30 assumes a residual standard deviation of 30 pp: restaurants' sales changes still vary around what is expected after adjustment. It does not mean they all grow 30 %, and it is not a figure measured at Just Eat. D = 1.5 is a scenario that multiplies the estimator's variance by 1.5 to represent additional dependence. Its uncertainty grows by √1.5 ≈ 1.22, not by 1.5.

The standard error, SE, measures how much our estimate would vary if we repeated the study. It differs from σ: σ describes variation across restaurants; SE describes the uncertainty of the estimated mean difference. With N restaurants in total, half in each group, we use this approximation:

$$SE \approx 2\sigma\sqrt{D/N},\qquad MDE \approx (z_{1-\alpha/2}+z_{1-\beta})\,SE.$$

$$N_{\mathrm{required}} \approx \frac{4\sigma^2D\,(z_{1-\alpha/2}+z_{1-\beta})^2}{\delta^2}.$$

The z values are reference points of the normal distribution: roughly 1.96 for α = 5 % two-sided and 0.84 for 80 % power. δ and σ are written as proportions: 5 pp = 0.05 and 30 pp = 0.30. N counts the restaurants of both groups together.

This formula is a planning approximation, not the definitive power of a staggered DiD. The final calculation must reproduce the real dates, the relationships between observations, the group sizes and the analysis weights. D = 1.5 does not replace that simulation. Good matching can also reduce σ.

This first calculation fixes σ to make the problem visible. In section 11 we will explain how it can depend on the customers observed and why we cannot yet treat 30 pp as a real figure.

Show reproducible code

for d in [.10, .05, .03]:
    requirements.append({
        "Efecto objetivo": f"{d*100:.0f} pp",
        "Total si D = 1": integer(required_total(d, P["sigma"], P["alpha"], P["potencia"], 1)),
        f'Total si D = {P["inflacion_varianza"]:.1f}': integer(required_total(
            d, P["sigma"], P["alpha"], P["potencia"], P["inflacion_varianza"])),

show_table(pd.DataFrame(requirements))

Under the current parameters, the sample of 1.040 restaurants no alcanza the objective of 5 pp con 80% de potencia: roughly 1.696 are required. The minimum detectable effect is 6.4 pp y la potencia para el efecto objetivo es 59%. It is a limitation of the scenario; it is not yet a conclusion about the real data.

How to interpret an imprecise result. Under the initial assumptions and with 1,040 restaurants, the standard error is about 2.3 pp. A 95 % interval would be approximated as estimate ± 1.96 × SE, that is, ± 4.5 pp. If a hypothetical study estimated +4 pp, we would get roughly [−0.5; +8.5] pp: a range compatible both with no effect and with a 5 pp improvement we might care about. That example is not a Just Eat result.

A confidence interval describes the uncertainty of the procedure: under its assumptions, roughly 95 % of the intervals built by repeating the study would cover the real effect. It does not assign a 95 % probability to the effect lying within this particular interval.

So not significant does not mean no effect. To rule out a relevant improvement we need enough precision, not just a p-value above 0.05. The p-value measures how incompatible the data are with the hypothesis of zero effect, under the model; it is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.

Doubling the noise requires roughly four times as many restaurants. So does detecting an effect half the size. More weeks can improve measurement, but they do not turn each week of the same restaurant into a new independent unit. Here we study detection against zero; demonstrating profitability or that a cheap alternative loses at most a tolerable amount will require a different decision criterion.

6.1. Two different questions with the same restaurants¶

Question A: what is the average effect across comparable restaurants? We can compare within each market and cuisine type and combine those estimates. A cell contributes part of the common answer. The losses from missing controls were already subtracted in the funnel; putting labels on whoever remains does not subtract them again.

To understand the weights, imagine 200 pizza restaurants and 100 sushi ones, split between treated and controls within each cuisine type. An average representing those 300 restaurants would give two thirds of the weight to the pizza effect and one third to sushi. That is a per-restaurant average; a different target, such as giving equal importance to each cuisine type, would use different weights and could have different precision.

With independent strata, equal σ and D, and balanced groups within each stratum, overall precision is preserved if we weight by their sizes. In the formula, s identifies a cell, N_s is its number of restaurants and w_s = N_s/N its weight. The symbol ∑ means summing the contributions of every cell:

$$SE_{\mathrm{global}}^2 \approx \sum_s w_s^2\frac{4\sigma^2D}{N_s} =\frac{4\sigma^2D}{N}.$$

The effects can differ and we can still estimate their average. That average does not describe each individual effect nor represent segments with no comparison. Different weights, variances or dependencies change the calculation.

Question B: what is the effect of each cuisine type or market separately? Now each result needs its own information. If we spread 1,040 restaurants across five cuisine types, each gets 208: 104 treated and 104 controls. Each result uses a fifth of the sample.

With a balanced split across K segments and the same noise and statistical assumptions:

$$N_s=N/K,\qquad MDE_s\approx MDE_{\mathrm{global}}\sqrt{K}.$$

For five cuisine types, √5 ≈ 2.24: the MDE goes from about 6.4 to 14.3 pp per cuisine type. The table also computes eight markets and forty crossings. These are alternative plans, not samples to be added together. The small segments of an unbalanced split would have less precision than the large ones.

Show reproducible code
segment_plan = [
    ("Efecto global ajustado", 1),
    ("Un efecto por tipo de comida", 5),
    ("Un efecto por mercado", 8),
    ("Un efecto por mercado × tipo de comida", 40),
]

for label, k in segment_plan:
    # Equivalent sample under a balanced split. A real run would use integer sizes.
    n_segment = N / k
    mde_segment = detectable_effect(n_segment, P["sigma"], P["alpha"],
                                    P["potencia"], P["inflacion_varianza"])

                                         P["potencia"], P["inflacion_varianza"])

        "Efectos a estimar": k,

    })

# Check of the global effect using the UNEQUAL sizes from the pair map above.
stratum_n = 2 * pairs[pairs > 0].astype(float)

pooled_mde = (norm.ppf(1-P["alpha"]/2) + norm.ppf(P["potencia"])) * pooled_se
assert np.isclose(pooled_mde, MDE)
for (_, k), mde_segment in zip(segment_plan, segment_mdes):

6.2. Many conclusions also change the statistical criterion¶

So far, α = 5 % applies to each question separately. If we ask many questions, there are more opportunities to get a result by chance. That is the multiplicity problem.

For example, if we test five cuisine types, there is no real effect in any of them and the five tests are independent, the probability of at least one false positive is 1 − 0.95⁵ ≈ 22.6 %. Independence is used only in this example; results for real cuisine types could be related.

A conservative solution is Bonferroni: splitting the total risk across the questions. For five cuisine types and a joint risk of 5 %, we use α = 1 % for each cuisine type: $\alpha_s=\alpha/K$. That keeps the risk of at least one false positive at 5 % at most, under valid tests, even without independence. Other corrections exist; this one serves as a planning reference.

The table asks for 80 % power for each effect, using that adjusted threshold. It does not promise an 80 % probability of detecting all the effects at once. And we do not need forty tests just because we adjusted a single global average using forty strata: what matters is how many conclusions we test, not how many labels we use.

With few restaurants per group, the normal approximation can be fragile. These figures flag problems of scale; the definitive power calculation must simulate the real design and sizes.

Show reproducible code
multiplicity_rows = []
for label, k in segment_plan:
    corrected_alpha = P["alpha"] / k
    required_corrected = required_total(P["efecto_objetivo"], P["sigma"], corrected_alpha,
                                       P["potencia"], P["inflacion_varianza"])
    multiplicity_rows.append({
        "Plan de conclusiones": label,
        "α por contraste (Bonferroni)": f"{corrected_alpha*100:.3f}%",
        "Total needed without correction": integer(k*per_segment_required),
        "Total necesario con Bonferroni": integer(k*required_corrected),
    })
show_table(pd.DataFrame(multiplicity_rows))
Plan de conclusiones α por contraste (Bonferroni) Total needed without correction Total necesario con Bonferroni
Efecto global ajustado 5.000% 1.696 1.696
Un efecto por tipo de comida 1.000% 8.480 12.620
Un efecto por mercado 0.625% 13.568 22.112
Un efecto por mercado × tipo de comida 0.125% 67.840 143.040

The decision determines the statistical question. To evaluate the programme as a whole an adjusted average may suffice. To fund only certain segments we need evidence about them, or we must evaluate that selection policy directly.

Another caution: one segment being significant and another not does not demonstrate that their effects differ. Both could estimate +5 pp, with one carrying far more uncertainty. Comparing their effects requires testing the difference between them directly.

A hierarchical model could share information across segments by assuming they are related. That option adds assumptions and does not create controls where there are none. We do not adopt it here as the next method: the alternative remains to be defined.

7. The horizon also consumes comparisons¶

The horizon is how long we want to observe the effect. If A publishes on 1 March and B on the 15th, we have roughly two weeks in which A has photos and B does not. When B publishes, that pair stops providing a comparison against a restaurant without photos. Even with a year of records, we do not get eight weeks of that contrast from that pair.

To study eight weeks we need controls that stay unpublished throughout that horizon, or a design and assumptions that identify the question some other way. The chart assumes that, as the horizon lengthens, we find fewer restaurants with an adequate temporal comparison.

We change only that availability rate and hold the noise σ constant to isolate its effect. In reality σ can also change with follow-up. The waiting rates in the chart are hypothetical.

Show reproducible code

    scenario = {**P, "contraste": rate}
    n = sample_size(scenario)

8. The result changes if the assumptions change¶

We still do not know how much noise remains or how many comparisons we will be able to keep. That is why we run a sensitivity analysis: we repeat the calculations under different assumptions to see whether the decision changes.

The favourable scenario assumes more requests, more valid comparisons and less noise. The restricted one assumes the opposite. All keep the same hypothetical universe, significance level and target power. The rates can be revised in the code of the following cell.

The second table changes only α: demanding 1 % false positives is stricter than allowing 5 %, and requires more sample to detect the same effect at the same power.

Show reproducible code

Asking for more sensitivity and asking for more certainty against false positives are different demands. Detecting 3 pp instead of 5 requires more information. Cutting α from 5 % to 1 % does too, but because we raise the bar for declaring an effect. Raising α makes it easier to declare results and increases false positives; it does not correct bias. These criteria must be fixed before seeing the results.

The favourable scenario allows the strategy to be viable. The working one shows why knowing the size of the platform is not enough: we need to know how many adequate controls there are, how long they stay without photos and how much variation remains after adjustment.

9. Where this stops being a good choice¶

So far we have mostly studied precision: how much the estimate fluctuates because of a limited sample and variable sales. There can also be bias: a systematic error from comparing restaurants that would have evolved differently. Increasing the sample can give a more precise figure without correcting that bias.

Diagnosis Consequence What we would review
Priority is given to those preparing unrecorded promotions We may attribute to the photos sales caused by something else Assignment rules and commercial records
Similar controls are missing in certain cuisine types The result does not represent those segments Which population retains valid comparisons
Controls publish straight away We only observe immediate effects How many comparisons remain at 2, 4 and 8 weeks
The sample does not detect the relevant effect at the desired power A non-significant result would be inconclusive Simulate precision with the real calendar
The treated gain orders that their competitors lose Their gain may not be growth for Just Eat Market outcomes and interference

We would ask for a restaurant-week panel: a table with one row per restaurant and week, together with requests, priority, shoots, publication and photo versions. We would add orders, revenue, prices, promotions and prior characteristics. We would start with a relevant year, with enough preceding weeks to establish the starting situation and study trends. Adding 2020 just to gain sample could introduce a context different from the current decision.

We would check for changes before publication, simultaneous campaigns, missing data, common support and competition. The uncertainty calculation must respect repeated restaurants, chains and related markets. We would choose a primary metric and contrast, and handle the multiplicity of the additional analyses. A test that fails to detect differences in prior trends does not guarantee they are parallel: it may simply have low power.

Finally, more orders do not automatically equal profitability. If the photographed restaurants gain 100 orders and their competitors lose 80, the net increase would be 20 in that example. We must weigh that additional margin against the programme's cost. Besides, closing the service leaves the photos already produced available and lets restaurants look for alternatives. The immediate effect of publishing is only one part of that business decision.

10. The first alarm: we need evidence for each decision¶

At the start, a universe of 200,000 restaurants suggested information would be plentiful. Then we asked for something more demanding: applicants from the same period, with comparable histories and a difference in waiting time that allows the effect to be observed. The working scenario keeps 1,040 restaurants.

We can still combine comparisons to study an average. But if we want to decide which types of restaurant to keep funding, the average leaves the individual decisions unresolved. Each segment has to contribute enough information about its own effect.

To make the comparison concrete, we fix this decision requirement: detect 5 points of additional growth in each of five cuisine types, at 80 % power and α = 5 % per contrast. This is an analysis choice; the brief does not require estimating each cuisine type separately. If management only needs the aggregate effect, its own precision calculation applies, without imposing the requirement of five independent results.

Under a balanced split, our 1,040 restaurants become 208 per cuisine type: 104 publish and 104 wait. The required benchmark is 1,696 per cuisine type, that is, 8,480 in total. The available sample covers roughly 12 % of that need, even before correcting for multiple contrasts. The MDE per cuisine type is 14.3 points: a real effect of 5 points would be detected at less than the 80 % power required. It is not impossible to detect; the design simply does not do so as often as we consider sufficient.

The alarm is real within the scenario, but it is not yet a diagnosis of Just Eat. The calculation depends on assuming a residual variability of 30 pp. Before discarding the retrospective study we should ask where that noise comes from and how much it can be reduced by observing many customers at each restaurant. The next section opens that second pass.

La cobertura es de 12.3% de la muestra requerida. Before discarding the design, we will check how much the residual variability can change.

The question that was missing¶

The global average and the per-cuisine decisions need different amounts of information. That remains true. What we still do not know is whether each restaurant contributes a very noisy change in orders or a fairly precise measurement thanks to its thousands of customers.

The figure of 1,696 restaurants per effect is not a universal property of the method: it combines a target effect, statistical criteria and a variability assumption. We are not going to erase the first calculation. We are going to open that assumption, understand it and recompute. That way we will know what the data would have to show for the design to be viable.

11. The second pass: many customers really can change the arithmetic¶

A restaurant with few customers can appear to improve or worsen because of a handful of purchase decisions. With many customers we measure its outcome better. But all of them remain exposed to common events, such as a breakdown or a competitor opening nearby. We need to separate individual variation from shared variation.

Hemming and colleagues study precisely what happens when the number of groups is limited and we can observe more people within each group. In their context those are, for instance, health centres; in our application, the group would be the restaurant. Their result is useful for planning precision; it does not demonstrate that our retrospective comparison is causal. Paper: Sample size calculations for cluster randomised controlled trials with a fixed number of clusters (2011).

From averaging customers to needing restaurants¶

In the simple model, the variance of a restaurant's average is:

$$\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_r)=\sigma_u^2\left(\rho+\frac{1-\rho}{m}\right).$$

Here m is the number of distinct customers observed per restaurant, σᵤ² is the variance of the individual outcome and ρ is the correlation between outcomes of customers at the same restaurant, also called the intraclass correlation or ICC. It does not measure whether they are all from the same country or cuisine type. A value of ρ = 0.01 does not mean "1 % of customers buy identically" either; it describes statistical dependence.

The bracket has two pieces: (1 − ρ)/m falls as we observe more customers; ρ stays. If customers were independent (ρ = 0), averaging m customers would divide the variance by m. If they all contributed the same information (ρ = 1), adding customers would not improve the average.

Let n₀ be the total number of people we would need if they were independent, for the target effect, the variability and the chosen criteria. Then the total number of restaurants required is roughly:

$$K\approx n_0\left(\rho+\frac{1-\rho}{m}\right).$$

K and n₀ add up both groups. The formula is equivalent to inflating the individual sample size by the factor 1 + (m − 1)ρ and dividing it among the m customers of each restaurant. We do not simply divide the restaurant count from the previous section by its number of customers: they are different units.

An example to see the limit¶

Suppose n₀ = 5,000 independent people and ρ = 0.01. We pick these values purely to understand the formula: n₀ has not been computed for the order growth in our case. With a thousand customers, K ≈ 5,000 × (0.01 + 0.99/1,000) = 54.95; we round to 56, with 28 restaurants per group.

The table and chart that follow show the improvement and its limit. They assume groups of equal size, independent of each other, two balanced arms and a normal approximation, without before/after. The ICC values are scenarios, not estimates from Just Eat. Unequal sizes, few groups, users visiting several restaurants or dependence between markets all require adapting the calculation.

Show reproducible code
# Hemming illustration: n0 is the TOTAL of independent people, not restaurants.
HEMMING = dict(n0=5_000, rho=.01)

def cluster_requirement(n0, rho, m):
    raw = n0 * (rho + (1-rho)/np.asarray(m))
    return 2*np.ceil(raw/2).astype(int)

client_counts = [100, 1_000, 10_000]
hemming_rows = []
for m in client_counts:
    k = int(cluster_requirement(HEMMING['n0'], HEMMING['rho'], m))
    hemming_rows.append({
        'Clientes por restaurante': integer(m),
        'Restaurantes totales': integer(k),
        'Restaurantes por grupo': integer(k//2),
        'Clientes observados en total': integer(k*m),
    })
show_table(pd.DataFrame(hemming_rows))

m_grid = np.geomspace(10, 10_000, 300)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10.5, 5.8))
for rho, color in [(.01, TEAL), (.03, ORANGE), (.05, RED)]:
    raw = HEMMING['n0']*(rho + (1-rho)/m_grid)
    ax.plot(m_grid, raw, color=color, lw=2.5, label=f'ICC = {rho:.2f}')
    ax.axhline(HEMMING['n0']*rho, color=color, lw=.8, ls=':', alpha=.65)
for m in client_counts:
    k = int(cluster_requirement(HEMMING['n0'], HEMMING['rho'], m))
    ax.scatter(m, k, color=TEAL, s=50, zorder=5)
    ax.annotate(f'{integer(k)} restaurantes', (m,k), xytext=(-2,16),
                textcoords='offset points', ha='right' if m==10_000 else 'left',
                fontsize=9, color=TEAL,
                bbox=dict(facecolor=BG, edgecolor='none', pad=1))
ax.set(xscale='log', xlim=(10,15_000), ylim=(0,780),
       xlabel='Distinct customers per restaurant · logarithmic scale',
       ylabel='Restaurantes necesarios en total')
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(lambda x,_:integer(x)))
ax.set_title('More customers help, but the gain runs out\nShared dependence sets the limit', pad=16)
ax.grid(color=GRID, alpha=.8)
ax.legend(title='Within-restaurant correlation', loc='upper right', fontsize=9, title_fontsize=9)
finish(fig, '10_clientes_y_restaurantes',
       'Planning illustration · n₀ = 5,000 independent people · Dotted lines: theoretical limits · Not a DiD')
display(Markdown(
    '**La mejora puede ser importante:** en este ejemplo pasar de 100 a 1.000 clientes reduce la necesidad '
    'de 100 a 56 restaurantes. Pasar a 10.000 solo la reduce a 52. '
    'The continuous limit approaches n₀ρ = **50 restaurants**; that is not the same as guaranteeing power with 50. '
    'In exchange for needing fewer restaurants, we observe more people in total.'
))
assert [int(cluster_requirement(5_000,.01,m)) for m in client_counts] == [100,56,52]
assert np.isclose(HEMMING['n0']*HEMMING['rho'],50)
Clientes por restaurante Restaurantes totales Restaurantes por grupo Clientes observados en total
100 100 50 10.000
1.000 56 28 56.000
10.000 52 26 520.000

La mejora puede ser importante: en este ejemplo pasar de 100 a 1.000 clientes reduce la necesidad de 100 a 56 restaurantes. Pasar a 10.000 solo la reduce a 52. The continuous limit approaches n₀ρ = 50 restaurants; that is not the same as guaranteeing power with 50. In exchange for needing fewer restaurants, we observe more people in total.

11.1. Before/after can remove part of the shared noise¶

The DISC study, by Downey and Kenny, analyses following the same groups over time, even when the people observed within each group differ. Their basic model shows that a stable group-level difference cancels out when computing the change. In our case, a permanent advantage of the restaurant appears both before and after: on subtracting, that part disappears. DISC paper and mathematical development.

We do not need to require the same buyers to return. In fact, selecting only those who buy before and after would leave out customers gained or lost. We do need to measure outcomes over a well-defined population and watch for changes in composition. If we measure conversion, we would define eligibility before the relevant exposure; entering the restaurant listing can already depend on the photos seen in search.

The basic DISC model assumes the group's own component is stable. A restaurant can also have changes shared by its customers between periods: a breakdown, promotions or competition. Those changes do not cancel out automatically. Longitudinal designs require considering both the within-group correlation and its evolution over time. Hooper and Bourke, designs with repeated measurements (2015).

An intuitive way to represent the remaining noise is:

$$\operatorname{Var}(\text{restaurant change})\approx A+\frac{B}{m}.$$

A represents variation in the change that customers share and that the model still does not explain; B/m, the individual variation when measuring the averages. B collects the contributions from before and after. This is a simplified scheme, not an exact formula for growth with an estimated denominator: it assumes comparable numbers of customers per period and omits relationships that would need modelling in the data.

More customers reduce B/m. Comparing each restaurant with itself removes stable differences, but does not guarantee A is small. That is the connection between the number of customers and the residual standard deviation σ of our first calculations.

We do not count the improvement twice. Our DiD already follows the same restaurants: we would not additionally apply a "DISC discount" to its variance. If σ is estimated from changes computed using all their customers, the precision contributed by those customers is already included. Nor would we multiply again by Hemming's clustering factor. The illustrative D in this notebook represents additional dependence between the aggregate measures; in a final calculation it would be replaced by the estimated covariance structure.

11.2. Back to the decision: how many would we need then?¶

The available sample does not grow by changing the level of the rows: the scenario still has 1,040 comparable restaurants, or 208 per cuisine type under a balanced split. What can fall is the required sample, by measuring less noisy changes.

We still do not know A, B or σ. So we run a conditional calculation for the same order growth metric, without transplanting the 5,000-people example directly into our DiD. We keep the target of 5 pp, 80 % power, α = 5 % two-sided per contrast and D = 1.5. Only σ changes.

In the formula above, required N is proportional to σ². If σ falls from 30 to 15 pp, it halves and the required sample drops by roughly a factor of four. If it falls to 10 pp, the sample drops by a factor of nine. We do not know it will fall that way: we are computing what would happen if the data justified it.

The table gives the requirement per effect and for five separate effects. Power is computed using the 1,040 restaurants available for the average, or 208 for each cuisine type. Each per-cuisine result here carries α of 5 %; the joint control of false alarms is computed afterwards.

Show reproducible code

With σ = 10 pp, the scenario would meet the per-cuisine objective: we would need 190 por tipo de comida, o 950 en total, against 208 and 1.040 available. It is a conditional possibility, not an estimate of σ.

Under this approximation, the average requires σ ≲ 23.5 pp and each cuisine type σ ≲ 10.5 pp. Si los tipos de comida tienen distinta variabilidad, each type must be evaluated with its own parameters.

Si exigimos controlar al 5 % las falsas alarmas del conjunto de cinco contrastes, Bonferroni sets α = 1% for each. With σ = 10 pp we would need 282 por tipo de comida, o 1.410 en total. 12. The conclusion changes: first we measure the noise, then we choose the design¶

The story began with a huge universe and ended, in the first calculation, with an apparent shortage of restaurants per cuisine type. We now know which part of that conclusion was a hypothesis: σ = 30 pp. Many customers can improve measurement and reduce the required sample, although they do not create comparable restaurants nor remove the shared changes the model does not explain.

Under our initial assumptions, 1,696 restaurants are needed per effect; if the residual variability were 10 pp, the benchmark would drop to 190. That difference lets the same 208 restaurants per cuisine type go from insufficient to sufficient for the chosen individual criterion. We have not discovered that Just Eat has a variability of 10 pp: we have identified what would have to be checked.

The defensible decision is to keep the DiD as a candidate until comparability and precision are audited. The next piece of work with real data would follow this order:

  1. Fix the population, metric, horizon, relevant effect and false-alarm control before seeing results. Agree whether the effect that matters is per restaurant, per user or per cuisine type; those weights are not interchangeable.
  2. Reconstruct the dates and contemporaneous comparisons. Review service priority, anticipation, promotions, prior evolution, common support and possible losses or diversions of orders between restaurants.
  3. Use unexposed periods to estimate residual variability, differences between cuisine types, temporal dependence, restaurant sizes and repeat users. If individual characteristics are used, use the pre-intervention ones and keep the analysis question intact; do not adjust for consequences of the photos when we mean to include them in the effect.
  4. Calibrate power for the planned calendar and estimator. Compare the aggregate and the individual version, using simulations or resampling appropriate to the dependencies and explicit scenarios. Check false alarms under zero effect and sensitivity to changes of assumptions. That does not prove causality.
  5. If the comparison is defensible and precise enough, run the retrospective analysis. If comparability fails, another source of identification is needed; if precision fails, more information, a less disaggregated decision where useful, or a future design whose power is also justified.

Conclusion for the challenge. The platform can have many restaurants and still lack valid comparisons. But observing many customers per restaurant can substantially reduce the noise of the comparisons that do exist. Without measuring that variability we can claim neither that the DiD lacks sample nor that millions of records solve the problem.

A future experiment can improve causal assignment, but it does not guarantee power merely by being randomised. The next section explores an A/B test across users: it could exploit a lot of traffic, although its question changes when the restaurant also adapts its prices.

13. More users, but a different question: an A/B test of photographs¶

After assessing the comparability and precision of the retrospective study, we can consider another strategy: each restaurant receives many users; can we randomise which photos each one sees?

We would select restaurants that have professional photographs and an alternative version available. Group A would see the restaurant's own photos and group B the professional ones, keeping the same menu and the same prices in both groups. Each user would keep their assignment throughout the experiment, including when visiting other participating restaurants. Assignment would happen before the first relevant exposure, including the images that appear in search results.

We do not know whether Just Eat or the restaurants keep the earlier images. For a future study, we would store them before the professional shoot. The control has to represent a realistic alternative without the service. Restaurants with no photos of their own pose a different contrast — professional photos against no photos at all — which should be kept distinct from the contrast between two kinds of image.

This design asks whether showing the professional photos changes user behaviour at the prevailing prices. It can provide more randomised units, but we need to compute its power: repeat visits by one person are not independent users. Many users across few restaurants also fail to guarantee the result generalises to every cuisine type and market. Besides, both groups share preparation and delivery capacity; a demand increase causing delays could affect both.

Price reveals which part of the effect would be left out¶

The brief notes that restaurants could charge more for dishes with professional photos. It does not state that all of them raise prices, nor how often they do. But if photography induces an increase, that restaurant decision is part of the consequences of the service.

Imagine a dish that cost €12 and comes to cost €15 after receiving the photos. The restaurant decides its price; we do not change it. Our A/B test would show the old or new photos, always at €15. The table below contains entirely invented results to make the comparison visible:

Photograph the user sees Price of €12 Price of €15
Own / old Not observed in this A/B test Group A: 5 % buy
Professional / new Not observed in this A/B test Group B: 7 % buy

At €15, the difference would be 2 percentage points: 7 % minus 5 %. Under correct randomisation and the experiment's assumptions, that comparison identifies the effect of showing the professional photo at that price. The price increase is not automatically subtracted from the A/B difference, because both groups pay the same.

One question nevertheless remains unanswered: how many would have bought with the new photos if the dish had still cost €12? They might have bought at 9 %, say, and the rise to €15 might have reduced that conversion to 7 %. That 9 % is only an illustrative possibility: the proposed experiment does not estimate it. So neither does it estimate how much the price dampens or amplifies the result.

To assess the full change we also need to compare own photos at €12 with professional photos at €15, under comparable conditions. Observing historical sales at €12 is not enough on its own: demand may also have changed between periods. And lower conversion can coexist with higher revenue or margin, so we would measure those outcomes as well as orders.

What this alternative contributes. A user-level A/B test can measure the contribution of the images at current prices. On its own it does not identify the joint effect of offering the service and allowing the restaurant to adapt its prices, nor does it let us attribute any conversion drop to the price rise.

If we want to study that joint outcome, one option is to randomise the offer of the service across restaurants: some receive it now and others later, with both groups free to set prices. We would compare all restaurants according to their assigned group, even if some decline the offer. Price changes induced by the service would form part of the effect of that offer; we would not remove them through a statistical adjustment if we are after the total effect.

This option improves the causal justification against a non-random historical assignment, but it again requires enough restaurants and a design that accounts for competition between them. Changing the unit of randomisation changes what we can learn; it does not by itself demonstrate that we have solved the precision problem. The final choice still depends on the business question, the availability of photo versions and the power calculation for each design.

Part II makes this last option concrete. To incorporate competition between outlets, assignment will be made at a broader unit: a city or metropolitan area. The price of reducing contamination is having fewer independent units. We will have to compute it.

Part II · Designing the future before looking at its results¶

14. The first twist: a restaurant can gain without the platform gaining¶

Consider two restaurants competing for the same customers. After improving A's photos, A gains 30 orders and B loses 20. The platform gains 10. If we used B as A's control, the contrast would be 30 − (−20) = 50 orders: B was affected by the intervention too. Competition has contaminated the comparison. These numbers are invented; the mechanism is what matters.

The proposed solution is to randomise whole cities or metropolitan areas. Within a city, we also measure the restaurants that receive no photos: that way both the gains and the losses among competitors enter the result. If the reallocation happens inside that unit, the total captures it.

At Airbnb, Holtz and colleagues grouped listings according to the alternatives users consulted during their searches. Their experiment was about pricing, not photography; it serves as a design precedent. They compared individual and cluster assignment and found that clustering reduced part of the interference bias. It does not imply the same reduction would occur at Just Eat. Paper: published online 2024, 2025 volume.

Key moment: the unit of assignment must contain a sufficient share of the interactions the programme will change. The administrative label "city" does not guarantee that condition on its own.

Show reproducible code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10.8, 4.8))

vals = [30, -20, 10, 50]
ax.bar(range(4), vals, color=[ORANGE, RED, TEAL, '#B8C4C8'], width=.6)
ax.axhline(0, color=MUTED, lw=1)
for i,v in enumerate(vals):
    ax.text(i, v + (2 if v>=0 else -2), f'{v:+d}', ha='center',
            va='bottom' if v>=0 else 'top', fontsize=16, weight='bold')
ax.set(xticks=range(4), xticklabels=lab, ylim=(-32,65), ylabel='Cambio de pedidos respecto al contrafactual')
ax.set_title('El efecto sobre A y el efecto sobre el mercado son preguntas distintas', pad=20)
finish(fig, '12_competencia_y_total')

15. Before randomising, we define which service and for whom¶

15.1. A concrete policy proposal¶

The policy is granting access now to the usual professional photography service, against deferring that access until the main follow-up ends. Access means being able to request a free shoot, under defined conditions and operational capacity. It does not mean obliging the restaurant to receive a photographer, nor guaranteeing that every request ends in published photos.

As a starting point, we propose studying first shoots for already active restaurants, in markets where the service can be operated. Before the draw we would fix a cut-off date and consider eligible any restaurant that meets the operational rules, has not previously received this Just Eat service and has no shoot already committed. This is a proposed scoping, not a verified description of how the programme actually runs.

Having its own photos, or even good-quality images obtained elsewhere, does not automatically make a restaurant ineligible: we specifically want to assess the added value against the available alternatives. We would record its starting situation. Renewals, new restaurants and prior commitments would need another protocol or an explicit extension; we would not mix them in silently.

Starting situation City with access now City with access later
Already has programme photos Keeps them Keeps them
Eligible and requests Can be served under the fixed conditions Request queued; shoot after the main horizon
Eligible and does not request Still receives no shoot Still receives no shoot
Not eligible Keeps its usual situation Keeps its usual situation

Both groups can use their own photos or hire external alternatives. We also do not freeze prices. Substitution by other solutions and the price response are part of the policy being evaluated. The control requires being able to postpone new shoots without breaking commitments: that feasibility is yet to be confirmed. If both groups could use the service and only the reminders changed, we would be evaluating a different intervention, an incentive campaign.

15.2. Four variables not to be confused¶

For restaurant $i$, belonging to city $c(i)$, $H$ denotes the number of follow-up weeks fixed before starting:

Symbol Definition When it is determined
$E_i$ 1 if eligible; 0 if not Before the draw
$Z_c$ 1 if the city has immediate access; 0 if deferred By the draw
$A_i=E_iZ_{c(i)}$ Immediate access to the service By the rules and the draw
$Q_i, F_i(H)$ Requests; publishes programme photos before week $H$ Afterwards; these are outcomes of the process

If 10 restaurants have access, 6 request and 4 publish, all 10 remain part of the assigned group. Comparing only the 4 that published against those that did not would lose the protection of randomisation. This is the intention-to-treat (ITT) principle: analysing the assigned policy, including acceptance, refusals, failures and delays.

The offer, the communications and the photography package will be the usual ones that are up for funding. We would fix service times, budget, quality and queue rules before starting. An extraordinary commercial push or additional photographers change the policy; if included, they are described and costed.

16. A city is a starting point; the graph checks its boundaries¶

16.1. What we mean by an experimental market¶

We propose starting from cities and merging adjacent municipalities if they strongly share demand and delivery. We would assign each restaurant to a single unit, with boundaries fixed before the draw. The final unit may be a metropolitan area. We would not split an integrated market in two just to add more statistical units.

To check this we would use a prior period of searches and delivery areas. A choice session would be an episode in which a user searches for food for a delivery address and consults listings. Its end — an order or inactivity for a pre-set interval — and the rules on bots and repeats would be specified before the analysis. We would include sessions without a purchase: they reveal alternatives too.

16.2. From millions of searches to a matrix¶

Each restaurant is a node. For two restaurants $i,j$, we count sessions in which both were consulted: $n_{ij}$. If $n_i,n_j$ are their individual sessions, a candidate similarity is:

$$ s_{ij}=\frac{n_{ij}}{\sqrt{n_i n_j}},\qquad s_{ii}=0. $$

This normalisation reduces the mechanical dominance of very popular restaurants. It does not prove they are substitutes: searches, on-screen position and availability also play a part. We would combine the indicator with delivery-area overlap, links between chains and courier circulation. We would set activity minimums so that two visits are not read as a stable relationship.

A boundary measure for a candidate partition is:

$$ L=\frac{\sum_{i<j}s_{ij}\,\mathbf{1}\{c(i)\ne c(j)\}}{\sum_{i<j}s_{ij}}. $$

$L$ is the share of relationship weight that crosses boundaries. A low value is desirable, but it is not the same as a percentage of bias. Omitted relationships matter too. We would validate the partition on another prior period; the acceptable threshold would require sensitivity analysis, not a universal figure.

Airbnb used numerical representations of searches and hierarchical clustering; this simple matrix is our explanatory adaptation. Their appendix D compares thresholds of 250 and 1,000 listings: large clusters reduced precision but contained the alternatives better. It is a joint choice of power and contamination. The initial MDE for detecting interference was 17 % larger with the 1,000 threshold; they judged that containing demand better compensated for that loss. It is not a minimum number of users nor a power correction transferable to Just Eat. Detail of the choice.

Trade-off: grouping more competitors reduces external links, but leaves fewer units to randomise. Splitting into graph communities is an alternative if the cities are too large; it requires showing that the new boundary is still reasonable. We have not chosen that alternative as the main design.

Show reproducible code
exp_s = np.array([

 [.03,.02,.05,0,.7,.5],[.01,.03,.02,.7,0,.8],[.02,.01,.01,.5,.8,0]])

17. "Similar" means comparable before the draw, not identical¶

17.1. First we choose the population, then the pairs¶

Before matching, we would set requirements for reliable records, operational coverage and a genuine possibility of deferring access. For the relative metric we define later, the prior margin must be positive and far enough from zero. Its threshold would be set from prior information; if that excludes a relevant part of the business, we would prefer a metric in euros and recompute the design.

There is no universal number of inhabitants, users, restaurants or photographs that makes a city valid. We would assess sizes and expected exposure alongside the overall power. Requiring significant results from each city separately would be a different question and would need a different sample.

Priority Pre-randomisation variables Function
Operational context Country, delivery model, service rules Form compatible blocks
Outcome evolution Trend, seasonality and variability of the weekly margin Predict changes without the intervention
Size on the platform Margin, orders, active users, concentration by chain Control for scale, noise and concentration
Expected exposure Eligible outlets, existing photos, historical requests and lead times Compare the chances of receiving the intervention
Auxiliary Basket size, cuisine mix, population, tourism Include them if they help outside the training sample

17.2. A reproducible procedure¶

Within the same country/context, we build a small feature vector $x_c$. We standardise using the training period, $z_{ck}=(x_{ck}-\bar x_k)/s_k$, and define:

$$ d(a,b)^2=\sum_k\lambda_k(z_{ak}-z_{bk})^2,\quad \lambda_k\geq0. $$

The weights $\lambda_k$ are set in advance or chosen through temporal validation inside the development history. A constant variable is dropped; near-duplicate variables must not count twice. A regularised Mahalanobis distance could be used if their correlations should be taken into account. A minimum-weight matching algorithm looks for disjoint pairs with a small sum of distances. This is not the same problem as building the competitor network: the network defines boundaries; the matching looks for separate units with similar histories.

We would check the pairs on other weeks: is the difference in evolution still small? We would hold out a final validation period that is not used to select the best design. We would not tune repeatedly until we got a good result on that last period.

Google's guide for paired geographic experiments separates matching data, evaluation and A/A tests. It is an operational precedent; its advertising metrics and defaults are not ours.

17.3. What randomisation gives us¶

An independent coin per pair assigns one city to access now and the other to access later. We would store the seed, the list, the date and the outcome of the draw. Both start on the same date; if there are waves, both cities of each pair belong to the same wave.

Random assignment sustains the causal comparison; matching seeks precision. It does not require an observed parallel trend to hold exactly in every pair. A poor pair can add a lot of noise, even though the draw remains valid. Nor do we additionally need to slice every city by country × cuisine type × population and demand identity in each cell.

Show reproducible code

18. The effect we are after includes prices, take-up and competitors' losses¶

18.1. What we measure in a city¶

To avoid picking restaurants after seeing the outcome, we fix a set $R_c$ of active restaurants in each city before the draw. It includes eligible outlets, non-applicants and outlets with earlier photos. We follow their activity on the platform; a confirmed closure does not remove them. Orders are assigned once to the restaurant's city. New openings are described in an additional open-market analysis, with its own rules.

The weekly financial outcome is defined with Finance:

$$ M_{ct}=P_{ct}-C_{ct}, $$

where $P_{ct}$ is the platform's contribution after variable order costs, discounts, refunds and delivery under a fixed accounting perimeter; $C_{ct}$ is the cost of the photography programme attributed to that city. It would include shoots, travel, management and other incremental costs. It is not the total amount customers pay nor the restaurant's profit.

We would not deduct twice a cost already inside $P$. For a pilot we would charge the incremental costs incurred during follow-up. When studying a rollout or a shutdown we would distinguish avoidable costs, sunk costs and capacity costs: not all of them disappear when shoots stop being funded. The rules for allocating shared costs are fixed beforehand; alternatives are shown as sensitivity analysis.

With $B_c$ equal to the average weekly margin of the prior window and $H$ weeks since the draw:

$$ r_c(z)=\frac{H^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{H}M_{ct}(z)-B_c}{B_c}. $$

This is growth of the margin in euros. If it goes from 100 to 108, $r=8\%$. If a valid comparison attributes 8 % to immediate access against 3 %, the effect is 5 growth points. It is not a five-point rise in the profitability percentage on sales. We do not observe both outcomes $r_c(1),r_c(0)$ for the same city: the draw lets us estimate their contrast.

18.2. An explicit decision about the weights¶

With $G$ cities included, we can average effects giving each city equal weight, $\tau_{\text{city}}=G^{-1}\sum_c[r_c(1)-r_c(0)]$. That answers for an average city. To decide on funding we propose as the primary outcome the aggregate incremental growth, weighted by prior margin:

$$ w_c=\frac{B_c}{\sum_{\ell=1}^G B_\ell},\qquad \tau_w=\sum_{c=1}^{G}w_c[r_c(1)-r_c(0)]. $$

The weights are frozen before the draw. The euro equivalent over $H$ weeks is:

$$ \Delta_{\text{€}}=H\left(\sum_c B_c\right)\tau_w. $$

So the relative primary outcome and its translation into euros are the same contrast at a different scale, not two independent chances to declare success. The per-city average is shown as secondary. This choice settles something we had left open: the simplified city calculations will remain illustrative; the definitive computation must use these weights and real sizes.

18.3. Causal assumption and scope¶

We allow the treatment to affect every restaurant inside the city. To interpret $M_{ct}(z)$ as the result of a local policy we assume that assignments in other cities have a negligible impact. If that does not hold, the outcome depends on the full vector of assignments and this design does not directly identify "service everywhere" against "service nowhere".

We measure immediate access against deferred access, for first shoots, in the included population and over $H$. The control may anticipate that it will get the service later. Earlier photos do not disappear. We do not automatically identify a permanent shutdown of the programme, renewals, or the full long-run equilibrium.

Show reproducible code
exp_base = np.array([1_000_000,100_000])
exp_eff = np.array([-.01,.10])
exp_avg = exp_eff.mean()
exp_weight = np.average(exp_eff,weights=exp_base)

axes[0].axhline(0,color=MUTED,lw=1)
axes[0].set(ylabel='Efecto causal ilustrativo · pp de crecimiento',ylim=(-3,13))
for k in range(2):

axes[0].set_title('Base semanal: 1 M€ frente a 0,1 M€')
axes[1].axis('off')
